item.title: Accenture AI agents are sifting through applicants
item.description: Accenture is using AI across its recruiting process, although it maintains that final hiring decisions remain in human hands. Speaking to at its recent investor day, the global tech consultancy and outsourcing biz said it was using AI agents to sift through resumes (or CVs if you’re in the UK) and schedule interviews. Kate Clifford, global chief leadership and HR, said it was helping clients adopt a similar application of the nascent technology. "We call it frictionless recruiting, which is really our agentic recruiting solution. We put in an agentic recruiting solution where agents now do all the interview scheduling. Agents can screen a resume. We have assessments that deeply understand the skills of the candidates to help that process move much, much faster. Now a human always makes a hiring decision," she said. Clifford said the agent technology was used to help recruitment staff get through their work more quickly. "Our recruiters needed to spend time with candidates. They needed to spend time sourcing, but where they were actually spending their time was scheduling interviews, where they were actually spending their time was typing information into a system," she said. The executive claimed the agentic process reduced the time taken to hire for roles by 28 percent and improved candidate quality by 30 percent. AI agents also help new recruits get up to speed. Whereas it once took six months for an entry-level hire to become productive, the time has been cut to six weeks using AI agents, Clifford claimed, allowing them to produce billable work more rapidly. Accenture claims to serve around 9,000 clients — including some of the world’s largest businesses and government departments — with tech advice and services. For example, it won a contract with the US Internal Revenue Services worth $2.6 billion in 2023 . Any tech pro looking for a job with the company is likely being screened by AI as part of the process. The company also expects internal staff to get on the AI bandwagon. A memo sent to senior staff in February informed them that promotions to top roles at the corporation would necessitate "regular adoption" of AI tooling, and it is tracking usage. But not everyone is convinced by the value of AI in recruitment. A study published in 2022 found the idea that AI-powered recruitment software creates a fairer process was unfounded. A paper published in the journal Philosophy and Technology demonstrated that the software is little more than "automated pseudoscience." Tech job-hunters applying for a lucrative role at Accenture will be hoping the technology has moved on since then. ®

item.title: Domestic droid gone amok? Don't worry, you're covered
item.description: Two insurers are teaming up to launch what every high-tech homeowner may soon need: household insurance for robotic mishaps. Humanoid robots are tipped by some to be the next big technology trend, with industry figures like Nvidia's Jensen Huang predicting they'll be everywhere from factories to the home. But as with anything AI-driven, things can go horribly wrong, especially when automatons are roaming a home carrying out tasks. They have even been labelled as potential " botnets in physical form ." The timing may be apt, then, for the UK's first domestic humanoid robot insurance policy. Specialist insurer Adrian Flux is offering to cover British customers as part of its home insurance range, underwritten by Texas-based Tokio Marine HCC. The two firms say the product is meant to get ahead of an emerging market, with domestic robots expected to appear in UK homes from 2027. Demand has already appeared in the US, where robotics and AI companies have launched humanoid robots for the home , with early models costing around $20,000. These are less like the near-human elderly care robot in the BBC comedy series Ann Droid , and more like vaguely human-shaped machines. The policy covers damage to, and theft of, the robot itself, plus any damage it causes to the home or belongings. It also includes personal liability if the android injures someone or damages their property, and emergency recovery or safe disablement of the humanoid after a sudden or unforeseen malfunction, such as - perhaps - attempting to chop off your fingers or put your cat on the stove . “As robots start to arrive in people's homes, we wanted to provide clarity on who is responsible if something goes wrong," says Gerry Bucke, general manager for the insurance biz Adrian Flux. "Like the driverless car policy we launched in 2016, it will be updated as the technology and the risks evolve." Beyond the home, investment is pouring into humanoids across a range of applications. Chinese carmaker Chery using them as showroom sales staff , while another firm has demonstrated them in automotive manufacturing . Elon Musk famously predicted thousands of Optimus robots in Tesla factories by the end of 2025, but still believes its humanoid robot will be the company’s biggest product . ®

item.title: UK Shelly reseller warns payment data stolen after malware found on website
item.description: A UK-based reseller of Shelly smart home equipment has warned customers that their payment data may be compromised after “unauthorized software” was found on its website. “After receiving a warning from our payment provider, Stripe, we investigated and found unauthorized software on our website and server,” the email from Shelly Store UK, seen by The Register , stated. “We removed the identified malicious software, strengthened access security, applied security updates and introduced ongoing monitoring. We have also reported the incident to the Information Commissioner’s Office .” Shelly Store UK informed customers it was unable to determine whether their data was accessed or copied, although all customers who made orders during an unspecified window are being contacted. One punter told us that hours before they received the email from Shelly Store UK, they began a payment dispute with their card provider after a £221.28 transaction, dated October 26, was made in Australia using their details. They suspect their full card details were swiped at some point between October 12, when they made their first and only order with the company, and October 27, when they received the breach notification. Shelly Store UK did not immediately respond to our request for more details. Its notification email stated the internal investigation remains ongoing, and in addition to payment card details, customers may have had their names, billing addresses, and contact details compromised. Shelly Store UK recommended that customers contact their card issuer for guidance on whether they will need a replacement card, and to scour their transaction histories and report any suspicious entries. It also urged caution in receiving communications asking for data such as payment details and security codes, and recommended a password reset . “We’re sorry for the concern and inconvenience this may cause,” the company said. “We are taking this seriously and will contact you if our investigation identifies further information relevant to you.” Shelly Store UK is an authorized reseller of Shelly smart home products and is wholly independent of the main Shelly company. “Shelly Store is a reseller of Shelly and is not part of, owned by, or directly affiliated with Shelly Group,” a Shelly spokesperson said. “We do not manage the Shelly Store website, its business operations, and we do not direct our customers from any of our websites to Shelly Store UK.” ®

item.title: Google's search revenue Ferrari hits an AI-powered speed bump
item.description: Google is paying a higher price for its bet on AI than even Alphabet's $51.4 billion in Q3 capital expenditures suggest. The biz appears to have traded its high-performing search advertising business for the mediocre monetization of AI Overviews and AI Mode, a misstep that contributed to investor concerns as Alphabet lost roughly $500 billion in market value despite management's attempts to reassure Wall Street. Google's year-over-year search revenue growth slowed from 17 percent in Q2 to 12 percent in Q3 . It's still headed in the right direction, but at a slower rate. During Alphabet's conference call for investors, Douglas Anmuth from JPMorgan Chase & Co asked whether that's because Google is showing fewer ads in AI Overviews and AI Mode than it shows in its traditional search results. Chief business officer Philipp Schindler cited several reasons for that: foreign exchange rates, Europe's elimination of its customs-duty exemption, and "the lower monetization we were seeing in AI Mode." To compensate, Google said it is expanding the distribution of AI Overview ads and adding multiturn ads in the US for AI Mode queries. But some Google Ads customers appear to be more concerned about quality than quantity. In a social media post , Max Anderson, CEO of OnlyFinder, complained that Google has responded to declining search volumes by attempting to manufacture revenue growth through "short-sighted, highly extractive, customer-hostile tactics," such as charging advertisers more for lower-quality clicks, including clicks on search terms they had not agreed to target. Eric Seufert, an analyst with Mobile Dev Memo, dismissed the doomsayers in a blog post . "It’s tempting to look at the successive deceleration in Search revenue growth from Q1 2026 as a response to pressure from other chatbots and to assume that Search query volume is migrating elsewhere," he wrote. "But the earnings release notes that the 'year-over-year Search query growth rate [was] the highest it has been in the last five years' in Q3, so it's clear that Search usage isn't declining." So people are still searching, and the business is still growing, but less convincingly, thanks to the lower monetization of AI Overviews and AI Mode. And Google's answer involves more ads in AI interactions. Nate Elliott, principal analyst for AI at Emarketer, told The Register in an email that AI represents a double-edged sword for Google's ad business. "On the one hand, Google owns the thing that people use AI for most: search," Elliott wrote. "Our surveys say that by far the top reason people use AI is to look for facts and information. Luckily for Google, people also tell us they haven't stopped using search engines – they've simply added AI as a new behavior on top of search. item.title: Farm PC 'maintained' by a 14-year-old dumped support chap in a steaming pile of tech mess
item.description: Welcome to another instalment of On Call, the reader-contributed column The Register publishes each Friday as a cathartic service for readers who know that dealing with tech support BS can be a cow of a job. This week, meet a reader we'll Regomize as "Jason" who told us he had helped an agricultural equipment dealer with his computer issues for about 20 years. "One day this guy called me to ask if I could help at a farm in Yorkshire, where he'd arranged the supply and installation of a fairly substantial system that used a computer to do effectively everything for a few hundred cattle," he told On Call. "That meant individually feeding them, measuring milk yields, planning pregnancies, and periodically submitting all the data to the government." Jason said other tech support folk had tried, and failed, to fix the system. "This had somewhat soured the relationship between the agricultural equipment dealer and the farmer," he punned in his email to On Call. Well punned, Jason. But we digress. "Despite not being fond of wading around in cow shit at four in the morning, I agreed to take a look at the system," Jason told us. By this time he had learned that the farm produced many tons of milk each week, so assumed he would find serious industrial-scale tech once he reached the farm. That assumption was wrong. "When I arrived, the first thing that I found to worry about was that the whole thing was controlled by proprietary software on a single PC running Windows XP – just after Microsoft ended mainstream support." The other things to worry about were all acts of omission: the farm had no backups, no spare PC, and nobody on site to maintain the PC. Jason asked if anyone was responsible for keeping the computer up to date with the security patches and was told the farmer's 14-year-old grandson had done some computer studies at school, so he got the job. That lad had either not discovered, or deleted, the many rather racy videos Jason found on the PC. "When the farmer's wife learned of this, there was what can best be described as a hullabaloo," Jason told On Call. As he dug into the mess, Jason found that the computer was sending milk production data to Her Majesty's Government. He also found that neither the government, nor the farm management software vendor, had bothered to require installation of a firewall. Jason says he installed one, made a few other tweaks, and got the system working. "Everyone seemed pleased, or at least they did until they got my bill," he wrote. "And to be fair, they did pay it promptly." Jason never heard from the farm again. "I don't know if that's because it's still working OK, or if they're just too embarrassed to see me again, or they found someone cheaper who could cope with my recommendations," he wrote. What's the strangest or dirtiest place you've been asked to deliver tech support? Don't cheese us off by holding back! item.title: AWS installs an AI accelerator every 14 seconds and eyes $1 trillion annual revenue
item.description: Amazon Web Services will become a trillion-dollar business in five to ten years, and thanks to the AI boom Amazon CEO Andy Jassy thinks it should be able to grow by 40 percent or more in 2027 or 2028. The cloud giant is already on track to generate $184 billion annual revenue this financial year, helped by 39.3 percent year-over-year growth that propelled Q3 revenue to a whisker short of $46 billion. “It’s important to remember that the vast majority of global IT spend, about 85 percent, is still on premises, and we’re in a 10- to 20-year cycle where that equation will flip to the cloud,” he said on Amazon's Q3 earnings call. “Conventional wisdom has been that linchpin workloads like mainframes or storage area networks would never move to the cloud,” he observed, before triumphantly noting “these workloads are moving.” He thinks AI will help, too. Jassy said the cloudy concern installs a new AI accelerator “about every 14 seconds, and almost as fast as we install capacity, customers are gobbling it up.” The outfit’s Bedrock AI services is already the fastest growing multi-billion dollar service in its history, Jassy said. Core compute and storage services are also soaring: the CEO said revenue from both “grew at their fastest rates in several years.” Jassy thinks the performance of Bedrock and core services are intertwined, because when users select AWS for AI workloads they want their cloudy inferencing rigs to be “near the rest of their data and apps.” The CEO said AI workloads therefore “can’t help but drive core AWS demand because AI uses core for work like reinforcement learning, post-training, and tool usage, which can’t help but drive reinvestment back into our broader AWS functionality.” He thinks this scheme is already working because margins for AI services are already “well ahead” of the figures AWS was able to achieve for its core services at a similar time in their evolution. The company expects to make $220 billion of capital expenditure in 2026 and already spent $75.9 billion last quarter alone, most of that on AWS. Jassy said the cloud colossus is finding ways to more quickly pay for its infrastructure investments. The CEO said it’s not easy to do that. “I think what we’re seeing with AI, it’s the biggest transformation in our lifetime,” he said. “Would it be more convenient if this type of acceleration and opportunity happened over 25 years and you could spread the CapEx over 25 years? item.title: In the year AI re-wrote the infosec rulebook, it’s comforting to know crypto exchanges still have bad security
item.description: Crypto exchange Binance has paused trading after discovering unknown parties cracked one of its workers’ laptops and used it to make massive trades. Late on Thursday, US time, the company used its social media feeds to report “Our teams are aware of reports of a potential security issue and are actively investigating.” The exchange insisted “User funds are completely safe” and warned its customers “should remain cautious of scams and should not trust unofficial links, messages, or requests for account information.” The company soon froze $2.5 billion worth of assets and warned that the figure could go higher “as our teams work closely with law enforcement, issuers, blockchain intelligence firms and industry partners to trace and freeze additional assets.” To prevent the matter worsening, Binance halted all trading, deposits, and withdrawals. It also promised to cover any losses. About an hour ago at the time of writing, Binance posted an update on the incident that explains what it thinks went wrong. “Binance's initial investigation suggests that the security incident may involve a compromised DevOps engineer’s laptop, which allowed an attacker to gain access to a service container and submit unauthorized withdrawal transactions,” the post states. The company also hiked the amount it thinks is at risk to $6.3 billion and repeated its promise to cover any customer losses. The update also says Binance found no evidence of any wallet private key leak, suggesting that customers’ holdings remain secure. When they can use them again, as Binance is yet to resume trading. Binance hasn’t explained how attackers gained access to the engineer’s laptop. The scant details provided make it hard to rule out a successful phishing attack, or perhaps a supply chain attack on a package the developer used. Binance says it will spill once it knows exactly what happened. Cryptocurrency outfits have a long and inglorious history of falling victim to cyberattacks, perhaps starting with the 2011 raid on Mt Gox , to incidents allegedly perpetrated by nation-states , and, just last week, another situation possibly involving an AI-powered attacker . ®

item.title: PC chip plunge wipes out a quarter of Intel’s value
item.description: Intel’s share price sank by almost a quarter on Thursday after the company revealed a deep dip in sales of PC processors. The rout began after the silicon-slinger posted Q3 results that included some nice numbers, such as a 21 percent year on year revenue jump to $16.5 billion, helped by 78 percent growth for datacenter and AI products, and gross margins of 43 percent. The revenue number was at the high end of Intel’s revenue guidance of $15.8-16.8 billion, and the gross margin beat its predictions by two points. Outweighing those upsides was a decline in revenue for client computing and physical AI products, which saw incoming cash reach $8.1 billion but fall five percent year-over-year and nine percent decline from last quarter. In prepared remarks [PDF] published to coincide with Intel’s earnings announcement, CEO Lip Bu Tan said “In recent weeks, our customers began signaling a PC slowdown based on memory prices and availability. Year-to-date system end-point prices have increased significantly placing additional pressure on already limited IT budgets.” “The pace of the PC correction has accelerated over the last two months, as our OEM partners are aggressively managing inventory to match the softer sell through,” he added, before predicting that the market for PC chips will shrink by 12 percent next year and remain tough “until memory availability and prices begin to normalize.” Which may not be for years, given Korean memory-maker SK Hynix this week predicted that memory shortages will persist until the year 2030. Intel’s biggest business is therefore in trouble. AI and Xeons riding to a rocky rescue Tan tried to give investors reasons to be cheerful, by saying Intel sees a “resurgence in demand for CPU” sparked by customers’ desire for computing systems that consume less energy. “Increasingly, energy efficiency is becoming the most important metric for the AI infrastructure build-out,” he said. That matters, Tan argued, because “While GPUs are great at ‘thinking tasks,’ deterministic CPUs are far more efficient at ‘finding’ tasks. While a GPU reasoning query can run as high as multiple watt-hours of energy, a single CPU-based query could cost only joules of energy.” The CEO reasoned that lower energy consumption is important in the context of agentic AI – the idea that we will all soon run many autonomous agents to handle personal and professional scutwork. “Applying even conservative estimates to the total number of digital agents, and agents serviced per CPU, it is easy to anticipate a massive dollar and unit TAM [total addressable market] for CPUs over the coming five years,” Tan said. “By our estimates, server CPU TAM, largely driven by agentic workloads, could increase as much as 5X from where it is today, from $40B to more than $200B over five years.” But during its earnings call, Intel execs admitted it may struggle to cash in on that boom in the short and longer term as the company struggles to source key supplies like silicon wafe

item.title: Researchers find bugs in 5 AI developer tools, with OpenAI and Microsoft flaws still unpatched
item.description: Multiple vulnerabilities in five popular AI developer tools could allow attackers to execute code on a host machine, read and steal files, or spoof browser address bars. Researchers say flaws in OpenAI's Codex and Microsoft's VS Code remain unpatched, potentially putting developers who use affected configurations at risk. AI security startup Forever Security discovered vulnerabilities in Cursor, GitHub Copilot, Anthropic's Claude Desktop, VS Code, and Codex, and disclosed four of the flaws to the affected vendors. GitHub independently fixed the Copilot vulnerability without receiving a report from Forever Security. All five share a common security weakness: embedded browsers granted capabilities beyond those available to conventional browsers. Each tool “enriched its embedded browser beyond what a normal browser allows, and those enrichments undermined the traditional threat model - as agent input, as the authority on a tab’s own address, or as reach onto the host,” Forever researcher Gal Weizman wrote in a Thursday report . Forever dubbed this class of vulnerability “Embrace,” short for EMbedded BRowser, and said the flaws led to code execution in Cursor, data theft in Claude Desktop, Codex, and VS Code, and address bar spoofing in GitHub Copilot. Here’s what each of these looks like, starting with Cursor. Cursor: arbitrary code execution Typical web pages can’t run commands on the host computer because a web page’s JavaScript cannot talk to local apps. Cursor’s integrated browser, however, allows a page to call the agent’s composer. The agent reads this as instructions and follows them, but the instructions remain hidden from human users. This opens the coding agent up to prompt injection attacks that could allow an attacker to execute commands on the host machine. The researchers disclosed the vulnerability to Cursor on September 10, and the vendor silently patched the flaw on October 1. According to Forever, Cursor did not publish a security advisory about the issue or respond to the researchers' disclosure. Cursor also did not reply to The Register ’s request for comment. GitHub Copilot: address bar spoofing Under normal browser operations, a webpage cannot change the content of the address bar. “Copilot’s browser preview works differently,” Weizman wrote. “Some pages change their address without loading a new page, and the app cannot always see that. So Copilot let the page tell the app its own address.” The app checked only whether the text looked like a web address, starting with http, https or file, but it didn’t check where the tab really pointed to. This can be abused to trick the embedded browser into displaying a spoofed URL - such as github.com/login - in the address bar, while loading a fraudulent website - like a phishing page - underneath. item.title: Microsoft fixes a Windows 11 annoyance as PC revenue declines
item.description: Microsoft is beginning the rollout of a Windows 11 preview update that finally addresses a persistent power user complaint with the operating system: the right-click menu that obliterated years of muscle memory on command locations and hid others behind an additional click. The timing is notable, as the announcement comes alongside Microsoft's quarterly financial report, which showed a continued decline in the business of selling Windows licenses for new PCs. The preview update, KB5127936 , is cumulative for Windows 11 versions 26H2 and 25H2. The update will be a gradual rollout before eventually moving on to a normal rollout for all Windows 11 devices once it reaches general availability. The highlight of the new update should calm annoyed users who have spent years with custom scripts and services in an attempt to shape Windows the way they would prefer it. Users will get a "customize menu" button that controls what commands appear when they right-click their mouse. Users can toggle built-in commands such as Send To or Create Shortcut on or off, rearrange what appears on the main menu, and control which third-party extensions show up in either the main or submenus. The gripe with the right-click menu had been that Microsoft hid familiar command locations behind a top row of icons while moving other familiar commands under the "Show more options" submenu. Now, Windows users can customize the whole thing around their habits. The original Windows 11 right-click menu is a mess. Credit: Microsoft The new preview also highlights a new Windows feature called Cloud Rebuild, a recovery option that can reinstall Windows 11 directly from the cloud, even when an existing Windows 11 fails to boot. Cloud Rebuild will pull the Windows 11 image and needed system drivers directly from Windows Update. Users will not need a custom recovery image or external media to reinstall Windows. item.title: Howler will have AI answer your questions, then burn the chat
item.description: If you want to ask AI a question and watch the conversation go up in virtual flames when you're done, there's a new Mac app for that. Howler is an open-source app from a Chinese developer going by Aries Zhou, and it takes incognito mode AI questions to a new level by making them graphically interesting and easy to access right from the desktop of a macOS device. Anyone familiar with the Harry Potter series is likely to know where the name comes from - Howlers are letters that scream in recipients’ faces and then burst into flames, destroying themselves, which is the exact same thing the prompts ostensibly do once a user taps the Escape key. The Howler app displays a parchment-esque letter on the screen whenever the user presses Option+H, complete with a little wax seal that shows a letter representing their chosen model. Responses to queries are written out “at a hand’s pace,” per Howler’s website, first in glowing gold that settles to a sepia-toned print. “Besides needing translation at any time, I often want to look up a concept or learn about an event on the fly, without wanting to switch to a browser or open a separate session in Chat,” Zhou wrote in a comment on his Hacker News post showing off the applet. “So I made Howler, dedicated to Harry Potter fans, always there when you call, burning after reading.” The biggest catch to using Howler is that setting it up involves either using an AI service that can run commands, like Claude Code or another coding agent, or running the configuration commands manually. The recommended method involves pasting a setup prompt into the agent's input field. Once set up, Howler can connect to supported AI models using an API key, or to compatible models running locally. Howler’s website states that the API key never enters the chat and is stored in the macOS Keychain for safety. In addition to the API key for the chosen model staying local and not being printed, Howler is described on its website as only storing messages in memory with no history, sending requests straight to the chosen AI service and never through a relay, keeping no logs, and only connecting to an outside service to check for updates - and even that feature can be disabled. It’s a handy tool for those who want to ask AI questions without leaving a chat history on their Mac – like trying to remember the name of that damn function you’re supposed to have down by now, or whether Memorial Day or Labor Day is the one in the fall. Just don’t assume the AI provider won’t retain a record of the exchange. “Unlike regular conversations, it doesn't take up your conversation list, and you don't have to think about cleaning it up or archiving it afterward,” Zhou explained. “It's only for handling your sudden flashes of inspiration or a moment of confusion.” And it does it with panache - sure, it’s just an interface for an AI model one could find elsewhere, but it’s easily conjured, dismissed with a snap, and is open source, to boot. item.title: Startup wants to make AI agents safe for DevOps duty
item.description: Vera Platforms, a startup founded by researchers at the University of Michigan, believes there's a way to make agents trustworthy enough to handle DevOps. DevOps, which focuses on how software gets deployed and operated, is a particularly unforgiving affair. While AI agents have some leeway to make mistakes and correct errors as they generate code and work through a prompt, it's an entirely different matter when they make changes to real infrastructure running production workloads. "Live infrastructure is unforgiving," Ang Chen, CEO of Vera Platforms and an associate professor at the University of Michigan, told The Register . "An incorrect change can take down a service, open a security hole or erase data. Mistakes are often irreversible, and there’s no safe way to experiment: running code against production infra just to see what happens isn’t an option." For the past few years, Chen and his colleagues have been working on a way to benchmark agentic DevOps and a gym – a simulation environment – to help AI models get better at DevOps tasks. "From the research that we did, we've figured out various weaknesses of leading models," said Chen. "For instance, [Anthropic's] Claude, although it's very strong with Python generation, it just has some fundamental limitations that it can't get right when it comes to DevOps." An example of that, Chen said, is that when they asked Claude or OpenAI's Codex to decommission resources in the AWS cloud, the models didn't look beyond the default region. "The default region is us-east-1," he explained. "There are various regions in AWS, but Claude doesn't have this awareness that the cloud resources could exist in multiple regions, so it only decommissioned part of the resource." The fundamental reason, he said, is that these models have seen a lot of public code, but a lot less operational tracing. Vera Platforms aims to remedy the situation with three products: vera-gym, a playground environment that emulates production infrastructure; vera-bench, a test for measuring where AI agents fumble DevOps tasks; and vera-agents, AI agents that have been trained in vera-gym and are ready to be deployed for DevOps tasks. The CloudOpsBench test being released builds upon work done in 2024 that was presented at NeurIPS. According to Chen, Claude and Codex only score about a 50 percent pass rate. "It's a very, very hard set of tasks," he said. The test covers tasks like deleting decommissioned S3 buckets , repairing a compliance event pipeline , and restoring DynamoDB write autoscaling . "The tasks are authored by senior infra operators with many years of experience, with rigorous peer review," said Chen. This benchmark has the advantage of not requiring an actual cloud deployment. item.title: Topcoat enables Rust to render server-side web apps
item.description: Popular for other uses, Rust isn't typically deployed for web development. That could change, however. With AI here to do the heavy lifting, coders may want to consider the programming language, given its runtime performance and safety guarantees, suggested Carl Lerche , an Amazon Web Services principal engineer, speaking at ScyllaDB’s 2026 P99 virtual conference last week. Lerche was there to demonstrate his latest project, Topcoat , a framework for running web applications written in Rust. Lerche is perhaps best known for creating Tokio , which is the most popular asynchronous Rust runtime in that ecosystem. “Three years ago, had [I] gone out and said that Rust could be the best language for building web apps, you probably would have called me crazy,” he told the virtual audience. Web developers gravitate towards the languages they find most familiar. These days, that means JavaScript, or possibly Ruby. A number of web frameworks already use Rust. Both Leptos and Dioxus compile Rust into WebAssembly, which most browsers run. This approach is great for heavy computational jobs, though the upfront loading time can be a real drag. Topcoat compiles your Rust code into more web-friendly JavaScript. For Lerche, JavaScript remains the best way to interact with the browser's Document Object Model (DOM). “Generally, the approach taken by any Rust framework can be traced back to another ecosystem, usually a very popular one. You can't really point to a single existing framework as [Topcoat’s] main source of inspiration,” noted frontend developer Ken Kohlman, in a summary video on his “Code to the Moon” YouTube channel. Walk on the server side Lerche admitted that Topcoat isn’t for building complex applications, on the scale of, say, Figma, but it can easily be used for the run-of-the-mill, browser-based, database-driven applications, which is to say 90 percent of the web today. Unlike most present-day JavaScript frameworks , Topcoat eschews the current definition of being reactive, where the program logic is dumped onto the browser when the session begins. Instead, most of the logic executes on the server, with only the results delivered to the browser (Developers can still write client-side logic using a subset of Rust, which Topcoat automatically compiles into JavaScript for the browser). It’s an old idea recast with better tech. Server-side rendering predates reactive programming (see Apache’s server-side includes ). With server-side rendering, Lerche admitted, “It might sound like we're going back to the old days of full page refreshes for every click [but] you can actually get almost all of what you think of as reactive with server-side rendering.” But server-side programming has been making a comeback lately, especially for those devs disgruntled with React and other frameworks. item.description: Suspected Chinese attackers chained PHP2Shell with a Linux kernel privilege-escalation exploit to root 25 servers, including Palo Alto Networks firewalls linked to US government-affiliated organizations, according to Dream researchers. The snoops began exploiting these servers on October 23, targeting organizations across the US, Japan, Taiwan, and South Korea. The attackers also honed in on US government-affiliated firewalls. “Within hours of compromising a US government-affiliated firewall, they had tunneled into the internal network, compromised a third server using the same PHP2Shell exploit, and launched a full Active Directory attack campaign - all through a chain that started with a single unauthenticated HTTPS request to a management interface that should never have been exposed to the internet,” the Israeli AI cybersecurity startup said in a report. Plus, the attackers “likely still” have persistent, remote access to compromised organizations’ networks, Dream noted. The attackers rooted the first US government-affiliated firewall on October 23, but the device crashed shortly afterward, possibly due to around 900 MB of exploit traffic. According to Dream, it remained unresponsive despite 240 automated checks over two hours. They successfully exploited the second firewall a day later, on October 24. The compromised firewalls ran vulnerable versions of Palo Alto Networks' PAN-OS. Dream said it had been working with the vendor to investigate the compromises, and Palo Alto Networks' Unit 42 researchers independently verified the attacker's tooling and confirmed Dream's reported results. To break into the firewalls, the attackers built a custom exploit chain that includes PHP2Shell and a Fragnesia kernel flaw, and ran about 40 custom post-exploitation scripts once they were inside the targeted organizations. Total attack chain in under 15 minutes PHP2Shell , comprised of CVE-2026-109618 and CVE-2026-109619, came to light early last week, along with fears that attackers would abuse the bugs to take down most of the internet . Despite “hundreds” of PHP2Shell proof-of-concept repositories on GitHub, the first reports of successful attacks didn’t start until Saturday. Both bugs have CVSS scores of 9.2 and can be exploited without authentication to run code on vulnerable PHP servers. The PHP2Shell exploit recovered by Dream was not a copy of any known public exploit. It “appears to have been independently developed and tailored specifically for the targeted firewall platform,” the researchers wrote. item.title: Ubuntu 27.04 may bring a preview of the long-awaited Core Desktop
item.description: It's a few years behind schedule, but development has resumed on the desktop edition of Canonical's existing immutable IoT distro, Ubuntu Core. Engineering veep Jon Seager announced that Canonical is Accelerating Ubuntu Core Desktop on the company's Discourse forum. Even before his announcement, there was some fresh activity on the project's GitHub . The post gives some explanation of why the effort is running so late, envisions three potential use cases, and talks a little about the work that is already going on to enable it to finally happen. There's no solid timeline given, but Seager says that "over the coming release cycle" the team will be working out what needs to happen, which means that "over the coming weeks, we'll have the infrastructure ready for… daily image builds for Ubuntu Core Desktop." "Accelerating" sounds good, but with the best will in the world, it could hardly slow it down. In mid-2023 it looked like Desktop Ubuntu Core would arrive in 2024 , and at that year's Ubuntu Summit in Rīga, Latvia, it revealed more details . At the 2024 Summit, there was a talk about a KDE version – but no release. At the 2025 Summit, the Reg FOSS desk interviewed Seager and "Where's Core Desktop?" was our first question. The three roles his post discusses are the "browser-centric machine", a "developer workstation," and a "gaming machine." For this vulture, these goals imply two separate things. In general, this seems to indicate that it's wary of making something too specialized early on, then finding that it's not versatile enough for more challenging roles. Secondly, we think that the company is thinking of three specific niches that rival immutable distros have occupied successfully for years. Right now, the "browser-centric" one is filled by ChromeOS and ChromeOS Flex . We use Flex – it's pretty good, even if its days are now numbered due to the new Android-based GooglebookOS . Secondly, Fedora's Atomic editions have been around for years now – The Register first mentioned Fedora Kinoite well over five years ago. As well as Fedoras's own versions , there are also community-led distros based on the same tech, called Universal Blue . We've tried several, and while for now they offer nothing much this vulture wants, they undeniably work and they have happy users. Fedora's marketing aims at developers, and an immutable distro with containerized environments on top is harder to accidentally break with crashy work-in-progress code. Thirdly, the games-machine niche is owned by Valve's SteamOS . Although it is native to the Steam Deck – and if you're among the lucky few, the Steam Machine and Steam Frame – you are also free to run this on your own AMD-based kit . All three of these product families have been well-established for between five to ten years now. Canonical is lagging behind, and this is a subtle acknowledgement that it knows who the leaders are. item.title: BattMan aims to turbocharge US batteries without robbin' critical minerals
item.description: America's national laboratories are leading a consortium to move advanced battery storage technologies from the lab into domestic manufacturing. Dubbed the Battery Manufacturing Accelerator, or BattMan (no, really), the initiative aims to bring together a bunch of national laboratories, universities, and companies to overcome barriers in scaling up new battery technologies. Novel battery storage solutions are needed for applications in the electric grid, datacenters, and electric vehicles, as electrification gradually extends across industry. Batteries have a far lower energy density than fuels such as petroleum , so the hunt for better materials never stops. Researchers also want to improve on the safety of flammable lithium-ion cells , cut production costs, speed up charging, and reduce reliance on scarce raw materials. "The advances we make today in battery manufacturing technology will determine America's energy security and economic competitiveness for decades to come,” said Audrey Robertson, assistant secretary of Energy at the Department of Energy (DoE), which is overseeing the program. Researchers continue to develop new battery materials and chemistries, yet many promising technologies face obstacles on the way from the laboratory to commercial production. According to the DoE, BattMan will tackle that problem by combining super intelligence - known outside of the Trump administration as AI - with advanced manufacturing into a coordinated, data-driven innovation ecosystem. Pacific Northwest National Laboratory leads the consortium, along with Oak Ridge National Laboratory, Argonne National Laboratory and National Laboratory of the Rockies. Academic partners include the University of Washington, Binghamton University, University of Alabama, Arizona State University, and University of Michigan-Dearborn. The accelerator is also building ties with battery and materials manufacturers, and hopes to sidestep critical minerals supply problems by finding battery materials among more abundant, domestically sourced elements. ORNL is contributing its Battery Manufacturing Facility (BMF) R&D center and plans a smart test bed with advanced sensing, real-time monitoring, and data analysis to trial both wet and dry electrode manufacturing. BattMan will also introduce autonomous pilot lines that combine sensing, process monitoring and intelligent control systems to improve product quality and reduce variability in the manufacturing process. The goal is an AI-based manufacturing platform that spots production irregularities as they occur and adjusts parameters on its own to prevent defects. “The BattMan Accelerator is exactly the kind of coordinated national effort that turns scientific breakthroughs into economic and energy security advantages,” claimed distinguished R&D staff member Chins Chinnasamy, the consortium lead for ORNL. item.title: GSA left sensitive Google Drive files open to staff, contractors
item.description: A major US federal agency has repeatedly left sensitive information in its Google Drive accessible to employees and contractors who had no legitimate business need to see it, and auditors aren’t happy. The General Services Administration (GSA), which handles contracting, procurement, property management, and other elements of basic operations for federal agencies, has faced repeated findings of inadequate protection for controlled unclassified information (CUI) since at least 2014, according to a report from the agency’s Office of Inspector General. Again. Controlled unclassified information, in the US federal government's parlance, is information that isn't classified but requires protection or restrictions on its distribution under applicable laws, regulations, or government-wide policies. Access is generally limited to individuals with a legitimate government need to know. According to the OIG report, that can include things like physical security info for government buildings, personally identifiable information (PII) of government employees, and proprietary business information, all of which the GSA has left exposed. According to the report published this week, employees and contractors have approximately 2.5 million documents stored in GSA's Google Drive. “During a limited search of GSA’s Google Drive, we found 116 files containing CUI that were improperly shared with all GSA users,” the report notes. That’s a limited search, mind you, and the OIG has plenty of reason to believe there’s more than just that sitting open for anyone with access to the GSA’s Google Drive instance to sneak a look at. The OIG said that GSA is failing to properly manage the third-party tool it has in place to prevent data loss and detect CUI exposures, with annual reviews of search terms incomplete or undocumented, many relevant search terms not implemented, and a failure to enable an available optical character recognition feature that could help detect CUI in scanned documents. Additionally, the GSA was apparently “unaware of the tool’s file size limitation of 15 megabytes,” meaning that even if the GSA was properly using that tool, some large files would still be skipped. “We also found that GSA lacks: (1) an approval process for properly sharing sensitive information and (2) a standard naming convention that could more effectively prevent exposures of CUI in GSA’s Google Drive,” the OIG added. As for what was exposed … it’s not great. According to the audit, site plans for buildings in Washington, DC were part of the improperly access-controlled files, with data that includes entrances and screening techniques, as well as the location of sensitive areas, like gun lockers. A progressive collapse analysis that "describes the building’s collapse vulnerabilities, defense vulnerabilities, and critical failure locations” was also exposed. item.title: Oracle wants to bill you for every AI task, not just every seat
item.description: Oracle expects to earn more from existing application customers as it embeds AI in its enterprise software suite. Speaking at Big Red's investor day on Wednesday, Chris Leone, executive veep of application development, said Oracle will layer usage-based revenue on top of its subscription model. “The more work that gets done by AI in our system, the more revenue we will see because they're consuming AI units as that work is getting done. We don't have to add more seats in order for us to now generate more revenue,” he said. Earlier this month, Oracle revealed its Fusion Claw runtime , designed to help customers control AI agents that automate business processes. It targets ERP, finance, and supply chain management in cloud-based Fusion applications running on Oracle Cloud Infrastructure (OCI). Customers will pay for more work done inside Oracle applications, and Leone said Fusion Claw will also automate work done outside of Fusion. The promise of more revenue for Oracle, and higher bills for customers, came as the company sought to reassure investors about its spending, borrowing and revenue as it chases a share of the AI market. Oracle is funding a datacenter spending spree with negative cashflow and borrowing. OCI is set to host large language model builders, notably OpenAI, alongside its own customers' workloads. Oracle spent $55.7 billion on datacenters and cloud infrastructure in fiscal year 2026, which ended in May, and plans to spend between $90 billion and $95 billion in fiscal 2027. That will require more debt. In 2027, Oracle hopes to raise around $40 billion in debt and equity, on top of the $18 billion in debt it raised in September 2025. In a notice to investors this week, Oracle said it expects fiscal 2030 revenue of $225 billion, a compound annual growth rate of 35 percent from 2026. It expects positive cash flow by the second half of fiscal 2028, with capital spending falling the following financial year. Investors reacted positively. Oracle co-CEO Mike Sicilia also told shareholders the company will use AI to help implement its software, a plan he called as important as putting AI in the software itself. He argued AI will cut implementation time, bringing existing and new customers to OCI faster and boosting revenue. "On-premises customers can now move far more easily to the cloud by leveraging the AI tool sets to automate migrations and decrease the cost and time to implement. They don't have to be Oracle customers; they can be competitive customers." Sicilia said enterprise application software users' reluctance to change had been a major "headwind" for Oracle, one he hopes AI will ease. "Our large remaining base of on-premises customers are going to start to adopt this technology quite quickly. When we move customers from on-premises to cloud, we see a multiple increase in revenue," he said. ®

item.title: What is it like to work when your co-workers are AI agents?
item.description: Using AI for roles from executive assistants to chiefs of staff, companies are boasting about doing more with less, creating tension with their human workers On an average workday, Dhruv Amin chats with dozens of colleagues to get things done at his AI startup Anything. He might ask Gwen, his executive assistant, to schedule a meeting, then troubleshoot a technical problem with Cody, his coding partner. Then he might check in with Betsy for search engine optimization, or Juno for onboarding customers. If the office runs out of snacks, he sends a Slack message to Justin, the office manager charged with stocking the kitchen. But none of these co-workers are people. They’re artificial intelligence agents, software that handles tasks without human intervention. Anything is one of several startups building them, and betting on a future where workplaces will increasingly turn over their sales, marketing, coding and other tasks to semi-autonomous AI. At Anything, there are 15 human employees and roughly 150 agents – a ratio that Amin believes will soon be the norm. Continue reading...

item.title: Built to bend: Postgres’s inventor and a steward on what AI really needs
item.description: Michael Stonebraker introduced Postgres ® at Berkeley in 1986. Forty years later, the database he invented is a leading choice for a generation of AI projects, and he is among the sharpest skeptics of how those projects are being built. Bruce Momjian is cofounder and core team member of the PostgreSQL Global Development Group, and he works at EnterpriseDB (EDB). In upcoming episodes of AI & Data Horizons by EnterpriseDB (EDB), the Turing Award winner and MIT professor and the Postgres community advocate both make the case that the future belongs to systems that bend without breaking, and to communities that no single company controls. Zero, not 80 Stonebraker’s first exhibit is text-to-SQL, the promise that a business user can ask a question in plain English and get an answer from the warehouse. Public benchmarks such as Spider and BIRD report accuracy above 80 percent. His team tried the same thing on MIT’s own data warehouse—1,400 tables of student, faculty, building, and salary information—using real queries from its SQL log. “We got zero-percent accuracy. Not 80, not 70, not 40—zero,” he said. Adding agentic AI, retrieval, and prompt engineering lifted that level into the teens. Telling the model every table and join term reached the 30s. “Still not ready for prime time.” The reasons are the stuff of every enterprise estate. There is no training data, because the warehouse is not on the public internet. The data is idiosyncratic: among other things, MIT buildings have numbers, not names. The schema has rotted into cryptic table and column names and overlapping views. And real queries are harder than benchmark ones. His team has published its own benchmark, Beaver, and says nobody has broken out of accuracy levels in the 30-percent range. Use the model for what it’s good at The deeper problem, Stonebraker argues, is architectural. Large language models are good with text, but “what they are no good at is doing joins of structured data,” which is most of what an enterprise holds. Working with the city of Munich’s transport department, Stonebraker’s team found that answering a single citizen complaint about crosswalk timing meant combining regulations, CAD drawings, trolley schedules, and school-zone maps. Orchestrating that with a language model at the center was, he said, “ridiculously expensive.” The team’s answer, a system called Rubicon, uses models only on text, then casts the results into tables and hands the rest to a tabular engine. The orchestrator “looks like a query optimizer.” Stonebraker says it is cheaper by a factor of 10 and considerably more accurate than agent frameworks built around a model. He expects agentic AI to slide from the top of the hype cycle into the valley of despair before a more balanced view emerges. item.title: Belgium's tax agency confirms cyberattack, pulls services offline
item.description: Belgium's finance and tax agency has pulled "several" digital services offline after a cyberattack on the organization. FOD Financiën confirmed the attack on Wednesday, saying that MyMinfin, the agency's main online tax portal, as well as other online services, are temporarily unavailable while they start the initial investigations. "This measure helps limit the risks and makes it possible to carry out the necessary technical interventions to ensure the security of our systems," it said in a public announcement. FOD Financiën added that "this has consequences for tax deadlines in the near future," referring to the October 31 extended deadline to submit tax filings for specific types of income, such as sole traders and earnings from foreign companies. The agency confirmed the deadline will be extended to November 16, by which time MyMinfin, the platform through which such filings would normally be submitted, should be back up and running. The detail offered up in the public statement reflects the early stage of the investigation; not much is known, although there is nothing to suggest data was compromised. "Data protection is a top priority for the FOD Financiën," it said. "At present, there are no indications that a data breach has occurred or that data has been compromised. This aspect is also being closely investigated and followed up. "In the meantime, a large part of our other applications remains available with full or partial functionality. We are closely monitoring the situation and doing everything we can to make the affected services available again as soon as possible." Spokesperson Francis Adyns told local news outlets that the attack was thwarted within hours, and that it was unable to gain access to applications or data. "The attack could not be sufficiently expanded within our environment to take over applications or gain access to data," he told Nieuwsblad . "Elements that were potentially infected were isolated. As a result, MyMinfin, Tax-on-web, and Biztax went offline, but the hacking was successfully stopped. "The various services must be restored in an isolated environment. This requires considerable time to realize, with the necessary caution to rule out new risks." ®

item.title: Systemd adds support for Rust
item.description: Everyone's favorite Unix init system is adding support for the Unix world's favorite new programming language. What's the worst that could happen? Don't worry, this isn't here just yet. Agent P and his trusty team released systemd version 262 about a month ago. That means that systemd 263 is now under construction, and developer Christian Brauner announced on Mastodon that his new feature has been merged. The previous effort, which was pull request #44144, has now been split into five separate parts. Part 1 contains keyring-util and voa-util , described as "helpers for enrolling certificates into kernel keyrings." Part 2, support programs written in Rust , is the banner item. Then come a few more: bind only the headers Rust code uses , wrap the libsystemd-shared helpers systemd-keyring-setup needs , and finally, add systemd-keyring-setup . There are several important riders to the announcement, and these are spelled out in the second PR: "Rust is only used for new leaf components. Existing C code isn't ported and nothing that other components depend on is written in Rust." In other words, before anyone gets too excited, this does not indicate the start of an effort to rewrite systemd in Rust. All it means is that new systemd modules can be written in Rust. The second bullet point will be more significant for existing Rust developers: "No cargo. Everything is built with meson." Cargo is the Rust language’s package manager and build system. It's the normal way to build Rust applications, as well as to distribute modules of Rust code for other Rust developers to use. However, systemd already has a modern build system. It's called Meson and it's not unique to systemd – it is also used extensively by the GNOME project and the Mesa 3D graphics library. Meson itself is written in Python and uses Ninja to manage the compilation process. Ninja was designed to build Chrome faster , and it's also used for Android . The third stipulation is that any Rust code must not use the standard library . For those more familiar with C, this may sound extreme, but it's normal for embedded Rust programming . The project documents the system requirements. It needs Rust version 1.85 or later. That's modest: that version was released in February 2025 , and version 1.99.1 appeared earlier this month. It also calls for bindgen version 0.71.1 ( from December 2024 ) or newer, and Meson 1.4.0 ( from March 2024 ). These are relatively old versions – for instance, it's the Meson version included in Debian 13). Brauner added an interesting little coda in a second Masto post : saying that the team would have liked to support Rust in the core of systemd, but currently, Rust’s support for dynamic libraries isn't quite there yet. It's perhaps worth noting that writing systemd modules in Rust isn't the same thing at all as calling systemd from Rust code. There are several tools for doing that, and they have been around for years: for example, the systemd crate first appeared in 2015. ®

item.title: Critical launch for Vulcan as ULA targets Friday the 13th
item.description: United Launch Alliance (ULA) has set a target date for its return to flight: Friday, November 13, for a Vulcan launch. The mission will send 40 Amazon Leo satellites into orbit. A pair of BE-4 engines will power the booster, along with six Solid Rocket Boosters (SRBs). A Centaur V second stage, propelled by two RL10C-1 engines, will complete the journey to orbit and deploy the payload. The launch is the first Vulcan launch for Amazon after eight deployments with ULA's Atlas V. It is also the first since the launch earlier this year for the US Space Force in which an SRB burned through its nozzle during the ascent, treating viewers to some impressive fireworks and controllers to some likely clenched sphincters thanks to a "significant performance anomaly." In the event, the US Space Force payload successfully reached orbit, but the Vulcan was stood down while ULA conducted an investigation. This wasn't the first time a Vulcan had had issues with its SRBs. A nozzle was shed during the second launch of the rocket in 2024. Things went OK with the third launch. But another problem on the fourth trek to orbit meant a stand-down was unavoidable. The workhorse Atlas V has continued deploying Amazon Leo satellites during the Vulcan's hiatus. Another 29 were added on a July 2 launch from Space Launch Complex-41 at the Cape Canaveral Space Force station. However, Amazon booked 38 Vulcan rocket launches – quite an increase from the eight Atlas V launches ULA has already performed for Leo. It is obviously keen to add more satellites to its growing constellation. The SRBs are Northrop Grumman units, and the six Graphite Epoxy Motor (GEM) 63XL units will each provide an additional 459,600 lbs (2,044 kN) of thrust at liftoff. That's assuming nothing unexpected burns through or falls off. ULA has not detailed the results of its investigation or any changes it had to make. ULA said: "The integrated team has made great strides in improving our understanding of the solid rocket booster (SRB) anomaly that occurred on the previous Vulcan flight and have identified several potential contributors which have been mitigated through design and process improvements to the nozzle. To support our customers, this upcoming launch will utilize the improved nozzle design, and additional testing and analysis will continue in parallel with the mission. By flying the improved design, ULA gains valuable flight data that validates these improvements and is the most beneficial path in support of all our customers." US Space Force and Amazon are ULA's biggest customers - and Space Force will be watching. ULA came second to SpaceX in contracts awarded by Space Force for FY25 to FY29 . ®

item.title: Massive leak exposes 41,000 DHS workers and undercover ICE agents
item.description: An unprecedented leak of Department of Homeland Security records has exposed details of more than 41,000 employees or contractors who work for the department and its constituent agencies. The records include email addresses, phone numbers, and office addresses, but also references to internal systems and sensitive information on undercover and surveillance programs. In all, the leak provides a map of how DHS is organized and how it operates. The records, which span DHS itself as well as seven component agencies, including Immigration and Customs Enforcement and US Customs and Border Protection, were last updated on August 19, 2026. The transparency nonprofit Distributed Denial of Secrets and cybersecurity researcher and journalist maia arson crimew previewed the data for WIRED, which they say they obtained from a group calling itself the Department of Peace. DDoSecrets published the archive, which it calls “Icepick,” on Wednesday. In a press release, DDoSecrets says the data is from DHS's Okta login system. In a note with the files, the hackers wrote, “They have our information, so it’s only fair that we have theirs.” Read full article Comments

item.title: Shortlist of age checks for the UK's under-16 social media ban is out, 'some' adults will need verifying
item.description: The UK’s comms watchdog has put forward four methods of checking netizens aren't kids – dubbed highly effective age assurance (HEAA) – as it prepares for the proposed under-16 social media ban. The regulator says some adults may not need to prove their over-16-ness to social media platforms that will make inferences about their age based on previous activity, but confirmed that "many" are likely to have to undergo the same verification process. Big Brother Watch's (BBW) Director Silkie Carlo said: "This plan for a government 'social media ban' is a national ID system by the back door. Both the government and Ofcom have admitted that children will get around the ban, which means the real effect will be normalizing adults and children alike to handing over their passports just to get online." Ofcom says four methods remain from the seven it initially outlined when the Online Safety Act (OSA) came into force last year. The seven were capable of verifying whether a subject was 18 years old, but there are fewer viable options for determining the age of 16-year-olds, it said today. The methods put forward include: Photo-ID matching: Checking information displayed on identity documents and analyzing the photo against a live image of the subject taken during the verification process Banking checks: An estimated 90 percent of 16-17-year-olds in the UK have a bank account, which they would have provided their identity documents to open. The information processed by the bank can be used to verify whether someone is aged 16 or older Digital ID services: An interesting entry, given how quickly these were circumvented once the OSA age-checking requirements came into force. These third-party services analyze a person’s photo once, and if it matches the age they claim to be, let them verify their age across other services Facial age estimation: A method that even Ofcom admitted isn’t quite reliable enough to be used on its own. The regulator said that online services can use technologies to analyze a subject’s facial features to determine their age. The same technologies also have a margin of error of a few years, so online services may wish to use a second method of HEAA to verify the results of this check. The three reserved for those aged 18 and above include credit card checks (only adults can have a credit card), mobile network checks (MNOs require proof of adulthood to remove content blocks), and email checks – using a subject’s email address to make educated guesses about their age based on the other types of services with which it is registered. Ofcom acknowledged that not every 16-year-old will have a form of photo ID, which is required for all four of its HEAA methods, so they will need to acquire one in order to access online services. item.title: Attackers turn GitHub issues into supply chain campaign against 61 public repos in less than an hour
item.description: EXCLUSIVE Researchers identified at least 83 attacks against 61 public GitHub repositories, including popular open source projects such as Google LangExtract, Trivy, Brave browser, and MLflow, in what they suspect is a coordinated campaign to execute commands in CI/CD environments and steal credentials and access tokens. It all happened very quickly, the Radware threat hunters said in an exclusive interview with The Register . Most (77) of the malicious items were published during a 43-minute time span on September 1, with the remaining six occurring within the next two minutes. “Our guess is that the final aim was a supply-chain attack in which the attacker gains credentials for the repo, and then he has the power to change the contents – the code – as he wishes” and then push the malicious changes to others, Radware VP and researcher Gabi Nakibly told The Register . Nakibly and fellow Radware researcher Zvika Babo say they suspect a single individual is behind this supply chain campaign. This attacker used 74 different GitHub accounts, many of which had legitimate development histories, meaning they were likely compromised. "Considering that dozens of accounts posted the same type of payload, on the same day, within a narrow time window, and to the same infrastructure, it is reasonable to assess that the activity was coordinated,” the team wrote in research shared ahead of publication with The Register . A novel attack chain They discovered the campaign while investigating prompt injection in GitHub – and they told us the attack chain is part of what makes this supply-chain campaign novel, and extremely stealthy. First, the attacker publishes an issue, pull request, or comment containing malicious commands hidden in HTML comments. This ensures the content is not visible in the rendered page. Plus, a GitHub event – like a pull request or issue – can automatically trigger a workflow if the repository is configured to respond to that event, meaning the attacker can be pretty hands-off at this point. “The workflow automatically is triggered within a second, and if the workflow is indeed vulnerable, then the attack is executed successfully,” Nakibly said. The workflow incorporates attacker-controlled content directly into shell source code, and the shell executes the hidden, malicious command, which hoovers up environment variables and attempts to exfiltrate those to an attacker-controlled server. While the researchers examined logs from actual runs, and told us they found two cases containing evidence that the malicious command ran inside the automation environment, they can’t definitively say whether the attacker successfully obtained repository write permissions, modified source code, or compromised downstream software. But they're trying. “The big picture is that the attackers are trying to find every possible way to get inside the repos to get credentials,” Nakibly said. item.title: LibreOffice's 'no AI' stance meets LLM-assisted code
item.description: The Document Foundation (TDF) says LibreOffice has no built-in AI features and that its core developers do not use LLMs - but community contributors face different rules. In a Fediverse post , someone who goes by the handle of argv[-1] highlights three LibreOffice commits this year that acknowledge the use of LLM coding assistants. Two of them – Inheritance when setting paragraph style font size to 100% or +0pt and Enable relative font sizes in Calc cell styles – date from April and credit Claude with helping identify the fixes. More recently, September's Add Copy Image button to screenshot dialog acknowledges using GitHub Copilot in VS Code to generate the BitmapTransferable class, while the copyButtonHandler method was written manually with LLM/code-completion assistance. This is hardly a fatal flaw – after all, it's getting hard to find any major FOSS project with absolutely no LLM-generated code in it these days. However, The Document Foundation says that the leading FOSS office suite is AI-free. As we noted when it released version 26.8 in August , we interpret this statement as a jab at its former development partner Collabora. Back in June, we noted that increased AI integration was a headline feature in Collabora CODE 26.04 . CODE is Collabora's web-based office suite, based on LibreOffice code. TDF – the primary maintainer and custodian of LibreOffice since its 2010 fork from Oracle-controlled OpenOffice.org – has made the absence of built-in AI a selling point. In September, it published a blog post declaring that no AI is now a feature . Meanwhile, on October 21, TDF announced 9.4 million downloads over eight weeks – excluding Windows updates and downloads of older releases, which are counted separately. The foundation acknowledged that the reasons for the growth are difficult to determine. TDF's direct response on Mastodon is dismissive: "Ah, another high-quality Mastodon discussion. Again: No core developers use LLMs. We rely on contributions from the wider community and don't explicitly list tools people can't use – but we do require people disclose when they use LLMs and generally discourage the practice. We carefully review submissions by contributors to make sure the code quality is good and that the patch author understands their own code. LLMs are prohibited for students. That is not 'slop'." In other words, TDF's approach resembles what some commenters have compared to the Debian approach : LLM coding assistants are permitted for some contributors, subject to disclosure and human review. For AI advocates, this is the only pragmatic response – which could be summarized as the "AI is just a tool" school of thought. However, since this admission does seem to contradict the very visible public no-AI message, some LibreOffice users are really rather unhappy. item.title: Night Plane review – join the jumbo jet to hell in this indie horror head trip
item.description: Liquid Static Studio; PC You take on the role of flight attendant in this clever and absorbing retro-style game that veers from daft horror spoof to genuinely disturbing There was always something creepy about the job-simulator genre. All those mindless automatons queueing up to use your bus, bar or bed store, or whatever workplace you are trapped in for the duration of the game. The endless repetitive tasks. The emptiness of the world beyond your corporate existence. Together, these elements scream existential terror … which is perhaps why we are now seeing a new indie sub-genre of job sim horror games, including Home Safety Hotline, Dredge and more recently, Grease Trap ’99, a Lovecraftian mystery set in a Scottish chip shop. Now, we have Night Plane, in which you take on the role of a flight attendant on a jumbo jet to hell. It all starts kind of normally. You turn up for the first day of your new job, meet your colleagues, then take your spot at the departure gate, checking in customers and being careful to root out anyone with invalid tickets. Once on the plane, you roll your trolley down the aisle, serving booze and inedible meals, and occasionally dealing with passenger complaints. item.title: Traces of new Pi hardware spotted in GitHub
item.description: The wait for a new Raspberry Pi Zero may be nearly over, judging by the raspberrypi/linux repository. Among the merged pull requests is one titled "Add device tree for Pi Zero 3 W and Pi 4A," suggesting new hardware is on the way, including a successor to the very long-in-the-tooth Pi Zero 2 W. The board launched five years ago. Its 512 MB of memory was hardly generous, but it offered considerable bang for the buck. At the time, we reckoned performance was closer to the Raspberry Pi 3 than the flagship Pi 4, but perfectly adequate provided you didn't open too many browser tabs at once. According to the source tree, as reported by Phoronix , the new board could use the Broadcom BCM271, up from the RP3A0 in the current Zero. If so, that would be a significant performance gain, though it's unclear whether the 1.5GHz clock speed of the Pi 4, which uses the same SoC, will be retained. Heat is a concern as the Pi 4 gained a reputation for running hot under load without active cooling, and it throttles performance when temperatures climb. A board as small as the Zero will have even less room to shed heat. Assuming that challenge can be met, it would be a worthy upgrade for the venerable Pi Zero 2. There is no word on how much memory it is likely to have – we can't imagine much given the current cost of RAM and the need to keep the price at least close to that of the Zero 2 W, which can still be had for around $18. The code also hints at eMMC storage is mentioned, but that seems unlikely to reach the finished product, probably because of the cost. Alongside the Pi Zero 3 W is a Raspberry Pi 4 Model A. Where the Zero 3 W is a clear upgrade, the 4 Model A looks more like a cost-cutting measure amid rising hardware prices. Model A boards typically have less memory, and no Ethernet port, and the 4A appears to have a single HDMI output rather than two. Things could change before any hardware ships. We asked Raspberry Pi if anything was in the pipeline, but the company said it had nothing to add. Enthusiasts will welcome an upgraded Pi Zero after more than half a decade, provided the price is right and it doesn't run too hot. At the same time, a cut-down Pi 4 carries the whiff of inevitability in an era of rising component costs. ®

item.title: Microsoft breaks New Outlook attachment opening with Edge Update
item.description: Users of New Outlook wondering where the option to open an attachment went have a culprit to blame – an Edge update. The issue underscores how interconnected things are in the Microsoft ecosystem. According to the vendor, an update to Edge 156 "unintentionally enabled an unnecessary configuration," which means some New Outlook users are unable to open email file attachments. An error stating the file cannot be opened also appears for some, along with an instruction to restart Outlook. However, the "Open" option goes away after the error is encountered. A workaround is to use "Save As" to save the attachment, and then open the file manually. Microsoft confirmed the issue yesterday afternoon in the advisory EX1528992, and early this morning began rolling out a fix to disable the "unnecessary" configuration. It expects that it'll take 12 hours for the fix to be rolled out, and users will have to close and reopen New Outlook to feel the benefit. The problem raises some interesting questions. While we'd understand how something unexpected in Edge might cause rendering issues in New Outlook, losing the ability to open attachments because of something an Edge update did is concerning and may make some administrators reconsider the blast radius of software updates. We asked Microsoft for more information about the "unnecessary configuration" and will update this piece should it respond. However, the incident highlights connections within Windows that might surprise users. In addition, it shows that, despite a woeful showing on the desktop market share front – although Edge recently "surged" to almost 15 percent last month, according to Statcounter, up from around 10 percent for much of the year – Microsoft's browser can still capture user attention. It's just not the sort of attention the Windows maker might have hoped for. It is also worth noting that Outlook Classic does not appear to be affected by the issue (according to Microsoft's EX1528992 advisory for Exchange Online). Impacted users could therefore temporarily add opening attachments to the list of things the old software does that the new software doesn't. ®
